narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile of your class that year, compared to an average around the middle of the pack among accepted students, signaled that you may struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor, but it worked in your favor. At 3.80 it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, which helped pull the prediction back toward passing. Unfortunately this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the other signals.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Like your third-year rank, being in the lowest decile here also pushed the model toward predicting failure.

Taken together, the model saw your consistently low class standing in law school as stronger evidence than your solid college grades, leading it to conclude you were more likely than not to fail the bar.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening the areas that hurt your profile. Consider retaking key courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience that demonstrates your ability to succeed. Once you can show clearer improvement in your class performance, reapply; the model will weigh recent positive changes heavily. (248 words)
